issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the other two memory items, which describe intrusive, sensory-dominated, repeatedly replaying trauma memories. That combination is not impossible, but with no other items indicating organized narrative access, the 'very easily' wording pulls in the opposite direction and is clinically inconsistent within this node.

issues.item: Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of mugging/robbery. 'Being around children' and 'Happy families' do not show a plausible thematic link to the reported trauma, and there are no accompanying threat or appraisal items to explain why these social/family cues would specifically trigger this patient's robbery-related PTSD.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
issues.explanation: 'I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation mainly links triggers and memory with maladaptive strategies, but the actual triggers and memory content given are socially/family themed and intrusive-image based; deliberate conflict-seeking does not fit clearly with those items and looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, triggers centered on children and idealized families are hard to link clinically unless there is additional trauma meaning not represented elsewhere. The memory items describe perceptual re-experiencing of the robbery, but these triggers imply family/child themes that are absent from the rest of the profile, making the trigger set feel disconnected from the trauma type.

Within the Triggers node, 'children present' and 'happy families' suggest a loss/family-comparison theme, whereas 'being criticised or corrected' suggests interpersonal shame or sensitivity. These could coexist, but together they do not form a coherent trigger pattern tied to a robbery, especially given no threat or appraisal items supporting these meanings.

'Happy families' is a weakly plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery trauma and is hard to connect to the accompanying memory items, which are purely sensory/reliving-based and suggest trauma reminders tied more directly to the event. It does not fit well with the otherwise robbery-linked trigger pattern.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers and memory to maladaptive strategies, but the selected triggers and memory items imply intrusive re-experiencing, for which suppression/avoidance is coherent; deliberate conflict-seeking appears clinically disconnected and unusually externalising relative to the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Kwame is a 58-year-old Ghanaian-born hairdresser who has been married for over two decades and runs a small barbershop in a mid-sized American city. He came to the clinic after his wife issued what she described as an ultimatum: either he sought help, or she could no longer watch him disappear into himself. His PCL-5 score of 72 reflects a presentation of considerable severity, and even in the intake session he sat with his hands pressed flat against his thighs, as though bracing for something.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Kwame was closing his shop alone on a Thursday evening when two men approached him in the narrow alleyway behind the building. One pressed close enough that Kwame could smell the alcohol on his breath - sharp, sour, unmistakable - while the other demanded his phone and the cash float from the till. When Kwame hesitated, one of the men grabbed him by the collar and shoved him hard against the brick wall, correcting him with a snarl: "Don't make me tell you again." They took what they wanted and left him there. He was not seriously physically injured, but he stood in that alleyway for a long time afterward, unable to find any words for what had just happened - not to call his wife, not to call the police. He stood, and he breathed, and he could not speak.

What has followed is a life increasingly organised around the residue of those few minutes. The memories themselves have a particular quality that Kwame struggles to articulate even now: they come as images rather than as narrative - the man's face too close to his, the wall's texture, the particular orange of the alley light - and they replay with a compulsive, film-like momentum that he cannot pause or redirect. Because the memories carry such vivid sensory force, they also carry their own triggers back into the world: the smell of alcohol on a client's breath, a man loitering too long near the shop entrance, or any moment in which someone corrects or criticises him - however gently - can be enough to pull the images forward again, sudden and unbidden, the film restarting. When that happens, Kwame's first instinct is to suppress it, to press down hard on the thought and refuse it entry, and he has also begun quietly withdrawing from people - clients he once chatted with easily, a brother-in-law who visits on weekends - as though reducing human contact will reduce the chances of being caught off-guard.

The shop itself has become the central theatre of his difficulty. Hairdressing is close work: clients sit inches from him, and some come in smelling of alcohol, particularly on Friday afternoons. When that smell reaches him, the images flood back and Kwame finds himself dwelling inward, rehearsing what he did wrong that evening - why he hesitated, why he was alone, why he hadn't locked the back gate. This self-blame rumination, which he cannot seem to stop once it starts, keeps the memory vivid and close to the surface, so that the next trigger - a client who jokes that he's cut it too short, a stranger who pauses outside the window - lands with even greater force. The loop has tightened over months: his attempts to suppress the memories and avoid people have, if anything, left him more sensitised, more alert to anything that resembles a threat, so that the triggers themselves now seem to multiply.

His wife has noticed that he flinches when she corrects him about small domestic things, that he has stopped attending their church's Saturday morning gatherings, that he sometimes sits at the kitchen table in silence for long stretches. She cannot reach him in those moments, and he cannot explain them to her - the words still fail him, just as they did in the alley.

What finally brought him in was not the flinching or the silence but a morning when he turned away a long-standing client mid-appointment, simply because the man had arrived smelling of last night's drink. Kwame had lost business before, but losing it this way - through fear, through flight - felt like a line he had not meant to cross. He is most afraid that this will not get better. He is most hoping, quietly, that someone can help him find the words.
